summary.text: A microbiome is the community of microorganisms that usually live together in a given habitat.
Researchers generally count bacteria, archaea, fungi, algae and small protists as members, while including viruses, phages and plasmids is more controversial.
Only a small proportion of microbes are linked to disease, most are essential for healthy ecosystems, and a healthy microbiome is essential for human health.

facts.label: Early research
facts.value: Began in microbiology in the seventeenth century

facts.label: Microbiota
facts.value: All the living members that form the microbiome

facts.label: Disease link
facts.value: Only a small proportion of microbes are tied to disease

facts.label: Biofilm discovery
facts.value: Leeuwenhoek's biofilms hinted that microbes live in communities

items.prompt: In 2020 experts sharpened the definition and separated two terms. How do the microbiota and the microbiome relate?

options.label: The two words mean exactly the same thing
The microbiota is a bigger group containing many microbiomes
The microbiota is the set of living members that form the microbiome
The microbiota covers only the members that cause disease

items.explain: The 2020 definition clearly separates the terms: the microbiota consists of all living members forming the microbiome.

items.prompt: A friend says every germ should be wiped out. What does research from the past century say about that?

options.label: Only a small share cause disease, and most are needed for healthy ecosystems
Most microbes are harmful and the helpful ones are rare
Microbes matter in soil but have no role in human bodies
No microbe has ever been shown to cause disease

items.explain: Research has shown only a small proportion of microorganisms are associated with disease, while the overwhelming majority are essential for ecosystems and a healthy microbiome is essential for human health.

items.prompt: Seventeenth-century researchers suddenly saw tiny living things in pond water and plaque. What made that possible?

options.label: Sequencing of DNA
Koch's idea of pathogenicity
Cloning techniques
The first microscopes

items.explain: The first microscopes opened up a previously invisible world and led to the identification of microorganisms.

items.prompt: Many microbes in a sample cannot be grown in a dish. What let scientists study their communities anyway?

options.label: Growing them in much larger flasks
Reading the DNA of the community directly
Killing the fast-growing species first
Counting the colonies on bigger dishes

items.explain: DNA sequencing, PCR and cloning allowed microbial communities to be investigated without cultivating them.

items.prompt: A farmer sees microbes living both inside and outside her wheat plants. Why should she care?

options.label: They only sit on the surface and do nothing for the plant
They matter only once the plant has become diseased
They play key roles in plant health and in food production
They stay in the soil and never touch the plant tissue

items.explain: The plant microbiota lives inside and outside plant tissues and plays important roles in plant health and food production.

items.prompt: A 1988 definition says a microbiome is more than a list of organisms. What else does it cover?

options.label: Where and how the community is active, its "theatre of activity"
The tools and methods used to count each species in a sample
The disease risk posed by every species in the community
The date on which each species was first named by scientists

items.explain: The definition refers not only to the microorganisms but also to their theatre of activity.
